catalog_citation: Peust, Carsten. 1999. Egyptian Phonology: An Introduction to the Phonology of a Dead Language (Monographien zur Ägyptischen Sprache 2). Göttingen: Peust & Gutschmidt. 368 pp. Author-released open access (Heidelberg digi; archive.org mirror).
catalog_locator: ch. 6 Prosody, §6.1 Word stress: §6.1.2 'Stress in Coptic: internal evidence' p. 270; §6.1.3 p. 271; §6.1.4 p. 272; §6.1.5 'How to determine the stress position in a Coptic word' and §6.1.6 'Phonemic stress in Coptic?' p. 273; p. 274; §6.2.1 'Coptic compounds with final stress' p. 275.
catalog_quote: [p. 273, §6.1.6] Coptic words are always stressed on one of the last two syllables. Since Coptic word stress is intermingled with vowel quality and quantity to a high degree, it depends a lot on the interpretation of the vowel system whether stress in Coptic is to be considered bound or free. Cf. the following possible (near-)minimal pairs from Sahidic: ... [p. 274] As long as the unstressed -ε is transcribed as /ə/ as it is here and everywhere in this book, these are not minimal pairs. In theory, we could propose an alternative analysis according to which ə is an allophone of the phoneme /e/. In the latter analysis, it would become possible to consider word stress as phonologically distinctive. ... KNUDSEN (1962: 197) decides to analyze it as non-phonemic. [p. 270, §6.1.2] Fortunately, internal evidence of Coptic clearly indicates that exactly one syllable in a word is marked. ... The short vowels η, ο, and ω can occur at most once in a word, i.e. in the marked syllable. ... (This does not hold true for borrowings from Greek.) ... Long (i.e. double) vowels only appear in the marked syllable ... [p. 273, §6.1.5] It is possible to determine the stress position for almost all native Coptic words especially from the internal evidence discussed in § 6.1.2. Sometimes data from more than one Coptic dialect must be taken into consideration.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Target list for Coptic holds one title, Säve-Söderbergh 1949 (Studies in the Coptic Manichaean Psalm-book: Prosody and Mandaean Parallels). It is a verse-metrics study (accent-group scansion of the Manichaean psalms, 3:3 rhythm, Mandaean parallels), not a description of word-stress placement, so: prosody-but-not-word-stress. No open copy exists: the two archive. acquisition priority low. What could be read: Guillaumont's 1950 RHR review (Persée, pp. 235-237 in full, saved) describes the metrical principle without any stress-placement rule; Drower's 1950 JRAS review is paywalled (DOI recorded). Best first-hand statement actually read in this search of works with stress in the title is Peust 1999 §6.1.6 p. 273 (already held by the project from our earlier reading): stress always on one of the last two syllables, position lexical/philologically recovered, phonemic status open; Steindorff 1904 §73 and Mallon 1907 §12 (held by the project) say the same. Note: the target file marks copt1239 as not in the catalog, but the tree holds an our earlier reading round-2 Coptic record (classification 'S2 outside the catalog's scope(lexical)') resting on exactly this Peust passage, and the egyp1246 catalog record is a back-projection of it; nothing found here changes that coding. All downloaded material and the bibliographicwith lines added to.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (365 pp., text; PDF page = printed page, confirmed by footers '273'/'274'). extracted text of pp. 269-274 read in full. At sec. 6.1.6 'Phonemic stress in Coptic?', p. 273, the text reads exactly: 'Coptic words are always stressed on one of the last two syllables. Since Coptic word stress is intermingled with vowel quality and quantity to a high degree, it depends a lot on the interpretation of the vowel system whether stress in Coptic is to be considered bound or free. Cf. the following possible (near-)minimal pairs from Sahidic..' The supporting lines at sec. 6.1.2 p. 270 are also there verbatim ('Fortunately, internal evidence of Coptic clearly indicates that exactly one syllable in…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every native Coptic word has exactly one stressed syllable, which is always the final or the penultimate syllable; the stressed syllable is the only one that can host the full vowels eta/o/omega and long (double-written) vowels, unstressed syllables having reduced e/schwa, so stress position is recoverable from vowel quality (two-syllable final window; whether 'bound' or 'free' depends on whether schwa is treated as a phoneme; Knudsen 1962 treats stress as non-phonemic).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described as such; Peust p. 154 fn. mentions a suggestion that Coptic may have had intermediate degrees of stress; proclitic/construct-state elements are destressed (Steindorff par. 76-78).
new_statements.exceptions: Greek loanwords: internal criteria do not apply, accentuation uncertain (sec. 6.1.5). Late Coptic pronunciation and Coptic loans in Egyptian Arabic retract stress from a word-final stressed vowel (sec. 6.1.3, p. 271). Compounds with non-final stress treated in sec. 6.2.2. Possible near-minimal pairs ('ahe 'age' vs a'he 'yes') discussed p. 273-274.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement for native words; Steindorff 1904 par. 76 (p. 37) adds that syntactically bound groups (construct state + noun, proclitics) are pronounced as one phonetic word with the stress on the last word, i.e. the domain is the bound group. Language is extinct; evidence is orthographic vowel distribution, manuscript accent marks, Late Coptic reading tradition and Arabic loans.
new_statements.identity_note: Peust 1999 describes Coptic across dialects (examples mainly Sahidic and Bohairic) and states explicitly (sec. 6.1.5, p. 273) that stress position is assumed not to vary across Coptic dialects or diachronically from Paleo-Coptic on. Steindorff 1904 and Mallon 1907 describe Sahidic/Bohairic respectively but give the same rule. Statement applies to native Coptic words; Greek loanwords are treated separately.

new_statements.quote: [preprint p. 18, sec. B2 'Coptic sounds and stress groups':] There was a clear contrast between stressed and unstressed syllables in Coptic: Stressed syllables may have long vowels or the vowel [o], but unstressed syllables were apparently confined to the vowels [a] and [ə]. [...] [p. 19:] The stress pattern that can be inferred from vowel patterns allows us to identify a prosodic constituent “stress group“ (called “bound group“ in Layton 2004: 22). A stress group consists of a noun or a verb root (always stressed on the last non-schwa syllable) preceded by a series of unstressed, phonologically dependent (“clitic“) elements which are typically grammatical morphemes

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement window as the catalog record (Peust 1999: 'always stressed on one of the last two syllables'): Haspelmath's 'last non-schwa syllable' yields ultima or penult only, since at most one final schwa syllable follows the stressed vowel. It adds (i) the domain (the stress group/bound group: clitic grammatical morphemes unstressed, stress on the lexical root or on a bound full-NP object) and (ii) an explicit predictable formulation (stress on the last full, non-schwa vowel). The catalog codes Coptic 'lexical' on the strength of Peust's hedge that bound-vs-free 'depends a lot on the interpretation of the vowel system'; Haspelmath, transcribing unstressed -e as /ə/ exactly as Peust doe…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sahidic Coptic (as reconstructed): one stress per prosodic 'stress group' (= Layton's bound group); it falls on the lexical noun or verb root, on its last syllable whose vowel is not schwa, i.e. on the final syllable, or on the penult when the final syllable has only schwa (written final -e or an unwritten vowel); proclitic articles, person markers, tense-aspect and relative markers are unstressed; only stressed syllables carry long vowels or [o], unstressed syllables have only [a] and [ə]. Stress is not written and is inferred from vowel alternations (eire 'do' vs r-nobe '(do) sin'). This is a right-edge, vowel-quality-conditioned (last-full-vowel) placement, hence coded weight-sensitive here; it is the 'bound' reading of the same facts that Peust 1999 (catalog) leaves open between bound and free.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned (each stress group has exactly one stressed syllable; no secondary stress discussed)
new_statements.exceptions: Verb roots in the prenominal (bound) state are unstressed and the stress falls on the following full-NP subject or object within the same stress group, with reduction of the verb's vowel (p. 19-20 exx. (51) peče-iêsous [pəkjə-je:sú:s], (51b); p. 22 (57) sôtm / setm- / sótm- 'hear', kôt / ket- / kót- 'build'); unstressed written <e>, <i>, <ou> were probably [ə], [(ə)j], [(ə)w] (citing Loprieno 1995: 50); Greek proper names in the examples carry stress on their own final full vowel (páwlos, mo:isé:s).
new_statements.identity_note: Haspelmath 2015 Part B describes Coptic in its Sahidic dialect (reconstructed pronunciation, Leipzig-Jerusalem transliteration); Part A is Middle Egyptian and says nothing on stress (vowels unknown). Lambdin 1983 is likewise Sahidic. The catalog record (Peust 1999) covers Coptic generally with Sahidic examples; Mallon 1907 held by the project is Bohairic.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement about where stress falls: Peust 1999 (catalog: 'always stressed on one of the last two syllables') and Haspelmath 2015 (root 'always stressed on the last non-schwa syllable' of the stress group) describe the same ultima/penult facts, and Steindorff 1904 and Mallon 1907 held by the project say the same (last or second-last syllable). The one divergence is of TYPE coding: the catalog files Coptic as 'lexical' because Peust says bound-vs-free 'depends a lot on the interpretation of the vowel system' and cites possible near-minimal pairs that dissolve once unstressed -e is written /ə/; Haspelmath (following Loprieno 1995 and Layton 2004, and using the same /ə/ transcription as Peust) states stress as predictable from vowel quality (last full vowel; unstressed syllables only [a]/[ə]) within a clitic-group domain. If the catalog wants one label, 'right-edge two-syllable window, position recoverable from vowel quality (last non-schwa vowel); phonemic status analysis-dependent' covers both sources; Haspelmath supports a quality-sensitive (weight-sensitive) coding rather than free lexical stress.

sources.quote: Mais il est infiniment plus difficile de préciser les lois qui président à ce rythme. Il ne faut pas se dissimuler la part d'incertitude qui entre, en particulier, dans la détermination des éléments rythmiques, c'est-à-dire des mots qui se groupent sous un même accent métrique. Et c'est là pourtant une pièce de base du système. [...] Le rythme régulier est ici 3 : 3, et c'est la mesure caractéristique des hymnes mandéens. [EN: But it is infinitely harder to state the laws governing this rhythm. One must not hide the share of uncertainty that enters, in particular, into determining the rhythmic elements, i.e. the words that group under a single metrical accent. Yet that is a basic piece of the system. ... The regular rhythm here is 3:3, the characteristic measure of the Mandaean hymns.]
sources.note: Describes Säve-Söderbergh's system as accent-group (stress-count) verse scansion, 3:3 in the Psalms of Thomas; says nothing about where word stress falls in Coptic words.

From the two open reviews read (Guillaumont 1950 RHR pp. 235-237, in full; Drower 1950 JRAS, landing page only) the book is a metrical analysis of the Manichaean Psalm-book: verse lines are counted in 'éléments rythmiques, c'est-à-dire des mots qui se groupent sous un même accent métrique' (accent groups), regular rhythm 3:3 in the Psalms of Thomas, with Mandaean parallels.
